<action type="say">
First, a couple of urgent checks:

1) Check for leaks now  
- Look inside the cabinet and around the pipe for any dripping, spraying, or bulging pipe.  
- If you see water leaking or a pipe that has split or looks “ballooned,” go turn off water to that area or to the whole house immediately (I can walk you through how if you’re not sure).

2) Don’t use an open flame  
- Do NOT use a blowtorch, propane torch, or lighter on the pipe or near the cabinet. That’s a major fire risk and can damage the pipe.

If the pipe is just frozen (no leak visible yet):

3) Open things up and add gentle heat  
- Open the cabinet doors under the sink.  
- Turn up the heat in the house if you can.  
- Aim a hair dryer or small space heater at the pipes on a LOW–MEDIUM setting, keeping it a safe distance away from anything flammable and never leaving it unattended.  
- Move the warm air slowly along the pipe, especially where it comes through an exterior wall or near cold spots.

4) Open the faucet  
- Turn the affected faucet on slightly (both hot and cold if it’s a mixer).  
- As the ice melts, you may see a trickle start; that’s good—keep gentle heat on until flow is normal.

5) Watch closely for leaks as it thaws  
- As soon as water starts flowing, keep checking the pipe and cabinet for any new dripping or spraying—sometimes pipes only show cracks once the ice melts.  
- If you see a leak, shut the water off right away and put a bucket/towels under the area.

A few questions so I can tailor this better:
- Is any water currently leaking inside the cabinet or under the sink, or is it just that nothing comes out of the faucet?  
- Do you know if the frozen section is plastic (PVC/PEX) or metal (copper/galvanized)?  
- What’s your rough location (city/ZIP)? If you’d like, I can also help you get a plumber out using your area and how urgent this is.</action>

<action type="say">
Got it, thanks—that helps.

Since you’ve got copper, no flow, and no visible leaks yet, here’s a focused plan you can try:

1) Prepare the area  
- Open the cabinet doors under the sink.  
- Clear out anything stored there (cleaners, paper goods, etc.).  
- Put down a towel and have a bucket or large bowl ready in case a leak appears when it thaws.

2) Turn on the faucet  
- Open the affected faucet slightly—both hot and cold if you have a single handle.  
- Leave it open while you work. A small trickle, if it starts, is good; it helps melt the ice and relieves pressure.

3) Apply gentle, directed heat to the pipe  
Focus especially where the pipe passes through/along an exterior wall or the coldest-looking section.

Options, safest first:
- Hair dryer:  
  - Set to LOW or MEDIUM.  
  - Keep it moving slowly along the pipe, a few inches away.  
  - Do NOT let it sit in one spot or blow directly on plastic/flexible supply lines for a long time.  

- Small space heater (if you have one):  
  - Place it safely outside the cabinet, blowing warm air in.  
  - Keep it away from anything flammable and do not leave it unattended.

You can also:
- Turn up your thermostat a few degrees.  
- If the cabinet is on an outside wall, you can tape a light towel or blanket loosely around the back of the cabinet (outside, in the room) to help trap warm air—but don’t block the heater/airflow completely.

4) How long to try  
- Give it 20–30 minutes of steady gentle heat, checking every few minutes:
  - Listen for gurgling in the pipe.  
  - Watch the faucet; a drip or trickle may start.  
  - As soon as water starts flowing, keep the faucet open and keep gentle heat on another 10–15 minutes to fully clear the ice.

5) Watch very closely for leaks as it thaws  
- Keep checking the pipe and cabinet floor.  
- Look and feel (carefully) along the pipe for:  
  - Beads of water forming  
  - A fine spray  
  - A split, bulge, or “blister” in the copper  
- If you see any of that, shut off water to that line or to the whole house right away and put a bucket/towels under the area.

6) When to stop and call a plumber  
Stop and get a plumber involved if:  
- You’ve applied gentle heat for ~45–60 minutes and still have absolutely no flow, or  
- You notice any bulging or cracking in the pipe, or  
- You’re not comfortable continuing because of electrical/safety concerns.

If you want, I can help you line up a plumber in Minneapolis and look for someone who does urgent cold-weather/frozen-pipe work. If so, tell me:
- How urgent it feels (okay today vs. need within a few hours), and  
- Whether you’d prefer someone who can come today even if it costs more, or are okay waiting for a routine appointment.

For now: go ahead and start with the faucet open + hair dryer/space heater on the pipe. Tell me what you see/hear after about 20 minutes—no change, a drip, or anything unusual—and I’ll help you decide the next step. </action>

<action type="say">
That bulge is a big warning sign—the pipe is very likely cracked or about to crack.

Do this right away:

1) Stop heating the pipe  
- Turn off and unplug the hair dryer and any heater aimed at the area.

2) Shut off the water  
- Look under the sink for shutoff valves on the hot and cold lines (small oval/round handles). Turn both fully clockwise to close.  
- If you don’t have working shutoffs there, go to your main shutoff valve for the house (often where the water line enters the building or near the water meter) and turn that off instead.

3) Depressurize the line  
- With the shutoff(s) closed, open the kitchen faucet fully (both hot and cold) and leave it open.  
- If main water is off, also crack open another faucet (like a bathroom sink) to let any pressure bleed off.

4) Prepare for a leak  
- Keep towels and a bucket/bowl under the bulged area.  
- It may already be cracked and just not showing water until it fully thaws—better to be ready.

At this point, you should treat that section as damaged and plan on a repair rather than more DIY thawing. Continuing to heat it can turn a slow leak into a full break once the ice melts.

Next step is to get a plumber to cut out and replace that section and properly thaw the line.

I can help you find and schedule a plumber near 55402. Tell me:
- How urgent this is: are you okay with water off until later today/tomorrow, or do you need someone ASAP (within a few hours)?  
- Is it an owner-occupied home/condo, or are you in an apartment/managed building (in which case you may also need to call building maintenance)?</action>
